concepts.label: Water as a Renewable Resource
concepts.cardText: Three-fourth of the earth's surface is covered with water, but only a small proportion of it is freshwater that can be put to use. This freshwater is mainly obtained from surface run off and ground water, which is continually renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle. All water moves within the hydrological cycle, ensuring that water is a renewable resource. Even so, it is predicted that by 2025 nearly two billion people will live in absolute water scarcity.

topics.title: Water scarcity and the need for water conservation and management

concepts.label: Causes of Water Scarcity
concepts.cardText: Water availability varies over space and time, mainly due to variations in seasonal and annual precipitation, but water scarcity in most cases is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups. A region may have ample water yet face scarcity, as many cities do. A large and growing population needs more water for domestic use and to produce more food, so water resources are over-exploited to expand irrigated areas for dry-season agriculture. Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water, so agriculture needs drought resistant crops and dry farming techniques. Farmers' own wells and tube-wells may lead to falling groundwater levels, affecting water availability and food security.

concepts.label: Industrialisation, Urbanisation and Water
concepts.cardText: Post-independent India witnessed intensive industrialisation and urbanisation. The ever-increasing number of industries has made matters worse by exerting pressure on freshwater resources; industries are heavy users of water and also need power, much of which comes from hydroelectric power. Multiplying urban centres with large, dense populations and urban lifestyles have added to water and energy requirements. Most housing societies in cities have their own groundwater pumping devices, so fragile water resources are being over-exploited and have caused their depletion in several cities.

concepts.label: Water Quality and Scarcity
concepts.cardText: Water scarcity is not only about quantity. An area may have enough water to meet people's needs but still suffer from water scarcity because of bad quality of water. Even where water is ample, much of it may be polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers used in agriculture, making it hazardous for human use. The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to give every rural household an assured supply of potable piped water at 55 litres per capita per day.

concepts.label: Need for Water Conservation and Management
concepts.cardText: The need of the hour is to conserve and manage our water resources: to safeguard ourselves from health hazards, to ensure food security, to continue our livelihoods and productive activities, and to prevent degradation of our natural ecosystems. Over exploitation and mismanagement of water will impoverish this resource and cause an ecological crisis with profound impact on our lives. Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal), in water stressed Gram Panchayats of seven states, aims to bring behavioural change in the community from consumption to conservation and smart water management.

topics.title: Multi-purpose river projects and integrated water resources management

concepts.label: Hydraulic Structures in Ancient India
concepts.cardText: Archaeological and historical records show that from ancient times India built sophisticated hydraulic structures like dams of stone rubble, reservoirs or lakes, embankments and canals for irrigation, a tradition continued by building dams in most river basins. In the first century B.C., Sringaverapura near Allahabad had a water harvesting system channelling the flood water of the Ganga. Under Chandragupta Maurya, dams, lakes and irrigation systems were extensively built. Irrigation works have been found in Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra). Bhopal Lake was built in the 11th century, and the tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi, by Allauddin Khilji in the 13th-14th century.

concepts.label: Dams and Multi-purpose Projects
concepts.cardText: A dam is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment. Dams were traditionally built to impound rivers and rainwater for later irrigation. Today they are built for irrigation, electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial uses, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding, so they are called multi-purpose projects, where the many uses of the impounded water are integrated. The Bhakra-Nangal project in the Satluj-Beas basin is used for both hydel power and irrigation; the Hirakud project in the Mahanadi basin integrates water conservation with flood control. Multi-purpose projects launched after Independence were seen as the vehicle for development; Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would integrate agriculture and the village economy with rapid industrialisation and urban growth.

concepts.label: Opposition to Multi-purpose Projects
concepts.cardText: Multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny and opposition. Damming rivers affects their natural flow, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, giving rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life. Dams fragment rivers, making it hard for aquatic fauna to migrate for spawning, and reservoirs submerge vegetation and soil. Floodplains are deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, adding to land degradation. The projects induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases, pests and pollution. Irrigation changed cropping patterns towards water intensive commercial crops, causing salinisation of the soil. Ironically, dams built to control floods have triggered floods due to sedimentation. Projects also cause inter-state disputes, such as the Krishna-Godavari dispute over diverting water at Koyna.

concepts.label: Sardar Sarovar Project and PMKSY
concepts.cardText: The Sardar Sarovar Dam over the Narmada River in Gujarat is one of India's largest water resource projects, covering Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. It is meant to meet the water needs of drought-prone and desert areas, providing irrigation to 18.45 lakh hectares in Gujarat and to the desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan. The Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana aims to give all farms access to protective irrigation: expanding cultivable area under assured irrigation (har khet ko pani), improving on-farm water use efficiency (per drop more crop) and introducing sustainable water conservation practices.

concepts.label: Traditional Rainwater Harvesting Systems
concepts.cardText: Given the disadvantages of and rising resistance to multi-purpose projects, many thought water harvesting was a viable alternative, both socio-economically and environmentally. Ancient India had an extraordinary tradition of water harvesting: people had in-depth knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types and harvested rainwater, groundwater, river water and flood water to suit local ecological conditions. In the hills, people built diversion channels like the 'guls' or 'kuls' of the Western Himalayas for agriculture. Rooftop rainwater harvesting was common in Rajasthan. In the flood plains of Bengal, people built inundation channels to irrigate fields. In arid and semi-arid regions, fields were turned into rain fed storage structures, like the 'khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'Johads' in other parts of Rajasthan.

concepts.causeChain: Disadvantages of and resistance to multi-purpose projects -> water harvesting seen as a viable alternative; knowledge of local rainfall and soils -> region-specific methods (guls/kuls, rooftop harvesting, inundation channels, khadins, johads)

keyPoints.text: Many thought that given the disadvantages and rising resistance against the multi-purpose projects, water harvesting system was a viable alternative, both socio-economically and environmentally. In ancient India there existed an extraordinary tradition of water-harvesting system. People had in-depth knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types and developed wide ranging techniques to harvest rainwater, groundwater, river water and flood water in keeping with the local ecological conditions and their water needs.
keyPoints.followUp: Why did people start seeing rainwater harvesting as an alternative to big dams?

checks.criterion: States that water harvesting was seen as a viable socio-economic and environmental alternative to multi-purpose projects.
Explains that people used their knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types to develop harvesting techniques suited to local ecological conditions and water needs.

keyPoints.text: In hill and mountainous regions, people built diversion channels like the 'guls' or 'kuls' of the Western Himalayas for agriculture. 'Rooftop rainwater harvesting' was commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in Rajasthan. In the flood plains of Bengal, people developed inundation channels to irrigate their fields. In arid and semi-arid regions, agricultural fields were converted into rain fed storage structures that allowed the water to stand and moisten the soil like the 'khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'Johads' in other parts of Rajasthan.

concepts.label: Tankas: Rooftop Harvesting in Rajasthan
concepts.cardText: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tanks or tankas for storing drinking water. The tankas were part of a rooftop rainwater harvesting system, built inside the main house or courtyard and connected to the sloping roofs by a pipe. The first spell of rain was usually not collected, as it cleaned the roofs and pipes; water from later showers was stored. Stored till the next rainfall, it was an extremely reliable source of drinking water when other sources dried up in summer. Rainwater, or palar pani, is considered the purest form of natural water, and underground rooms beside the tanka kept cool in summer. Today the practice is declining in western Rajasthan because the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal supplies plenty of water.

keyPoints.text: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly in Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all the houses traditionally had underground tanks or tankas for storing drinking water. The tankas were part of the well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system and were built inside the main house or the courtyard. They were connected to the sloping roofs of the houses through a pipe. Rain falling on the rooftops would travel down the pipe and was stored in these underground 'tankas'. The first spell of rain was usually not collected as this would clean the roofs and the pipes.

checks.criterion: Explains that houses had underground tankas connected by a pipe to sloping roofs, so rain from the rooftops was stored in them.

keyPoints.text: The rainwater can be stored in the tankas till the next rainfall making it an extremely reliable source of drinking water when all other sources are dried up, particularly in the summers. Rainwater, or palar pani, as commonly referred to in these parts, is considered the purest form of natural water. Many houses constructed underground rooms adjoining the 'tanka' to beat the summer heat as it would keep the room cool.

keyPoints.text: Today, in western Rajasthan, sadly the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting is on the decline as plenty of water is available due to the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some houses still maintain the tankas since they do not like the taste of tap water.

concepts.label: Modern Adaptations of Rainwater Harvesting
concepts.cardText: In many parts of rural and urban India, rooftop rainwater harvesting is being successfully adapted to store and conserve water. In Gendathur, a remote backward village in Mysuru, Karnataka, nearly 200 households have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting, and the village has earned the rare distinction of being rich in rainwater. In Shillong, Meghalaya, though nearby Cherapunjee and Mawsynram receive the highest rainfall in the world, the city faces acute water shortage, and nearly every household has a rooftop harvesting structure, meeting 15-25 per cent of its water needs. Tamil Nadu is the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses, with legal provisions to punish defaulters. In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation system carries stream and spring water through bamboo pipes to plants.

keyPoints.text: In many parts of rural and urban India, rooftop rainwater harvesting is being successfully adapted to store and conserve water. In Gendathur, a remote backward village in Mysuru, Karnataka, villagers have installed, in their household's rooftop, rainwater harvesting system to meet their water needs. Nearly 200 households have installed this system and the village has earned the rare distinction of being rich in rainwater.

keyPoints.text: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is the most common practice in Shillong, Meghalaya. Cherapunjee and Mawsynram, 55 km from Shillong, receive the highest rainfall in the world, yet the state capital Shillong faces acute shortage of water. Nearly every household in the city has a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure. Nearly 15-25 per cent of the total water requirement of the household comes from rooftop water harvesting.
